name: Orlistat

lead: Orlistat is a capsule that blocks the enzymes that digest dietary fat, so less fat from a meal is absorbed. It is used during cutting phases for gradual fat loss, and some in fat-loss forums described it as a replacement for ephedrine.

It inhibits lipase enzymes in the stomach and pancreas, so part of the fat in a meal leaves in the stool, and very little enters the bloodstream. Trials, including a 1998 European study and a 2-year US trial, found more weight loss than placebo, about 2 to 3 kg extra over 6 to 12 months in one summary. Weight loss is smaller than with newer injectable drugs.

paras: It is taken with meals: 60 mg Alli is sold over the counter, 120 mg Xenical by prescription. It is used alongside a reduced-calorie diet. It works less for people already eating low-fat, and some forum posters report diarrhea and little benefit.

Oily spotting, urgency, gas and loose stools are common, reported in more than 25% of patients in one review, especially after fatty meals. It can reduce absorption of fat-soluble vitamins, and the label warns against use after organ transplant or with cyclosporine.

angle.text: Orlistat is used during cutting phases to absorb less dietary fat, so fewer calories reach the body and fat comes off gradually. Trials show a few kilos of weight loss over placebo. Oily stools are a known effect, and it works less for people already eating low-fat.

lead: Orlistat is a gastrointestinal lipase inhibitor used with a reduced-calorie diet for weight loss in adults. It is sold by prescription as Xenical (120 mg capsules) and over the counter as Alli (60 mg capsules), and it works inside the gut rather than being absorbed into the bloodstream [1][2][3]. Reviews describe it as one of five or so drugs available for long-term obesity treatment in the US, with weight loss smaller than that of newer injectable drugs [4][5].

Trials such as the 1998 European multicentre study and a 2-year US trial found greater weight loss on orlistat than placebo [6][7]. Grokipedia describes an average extra loss of about 2 to 3 kg over 6 to 12 months [1]. The most commonly reported side effects are gastrointestinal, including oily spotting and urgency, reported in more than 25% of patients in one review [4].

In bodybuilding and fat-loss forums such as T Nation, orlistat is discussed as a fat blocker and was described in 2006 as a possible replacement for ephedrine [8][9]. Some posters report diarrhea and little benefit [10][11].

Rx and OTC depending on strength

paras: The Alli label states it is for weight loss in overweight adults aged 18 and older when used with a reduced-calorie, low-fat diet [3]. Grokipedia reports prescription Xenical is indicated for BMI of 30 or more, or 27 or more with comorbidities, and for adolescents aged 12 to 16 [1]. Studies have also examined its effect on liver fat in obese patients with fatty liver disease, on diabetes prevention, and on cholesterol [12][13][2].

Its appearance relevance is limited to modest fat loss. Users in forums discuss it as a fat-absorption blocker during diets and cutting phases, and several posters question whether it suits people who already restrict dietary fat [14][15].

A randomized placebo-controlled trial in obese patients (European Multicentre Orlistat Study Group, 1998) tested weight loss and prevention of regain [6]. A 2-year randomized trial in the US examined weight control and risk factors [7]. The 4-year XENDOS trial studied orlistat as an adjunct to lifestyle change for preventing type 2 diabetes in obese subjects [13]. Earlier reviews noted reductions in total and LDL cholesterol over up to two years [2].

Network meta-analyses of weight-loss drugs place orlistat among the less effective options relative to semaglutide and tirzepatide [16][5]. A 2023 randomized trial in Asian adults with obesity and fatty liver compared orlistat with a diet [12]. Other registered studies include trials on uric acid, polycystic ovary syndrome and maintenance after weight loss [17][18][19].

Reviews report oily fecal spotting, urgency and other gastrointestinal effects in more than 25% of patients [4]. Grokipedia adds flatulence and steatorrhea, with dose dependence, and notes that fat-soluble vitamin absorption can be affected, so a multivitamin is advised [1].

The OTC label contains warnings: do not use after organ transplant, with cyclosporine, in people with food-absorption problems, or if allergic to ingredients; ask a doctor if there is a history of gallbladder problems, kidney stones or pancreatitis [3].

Orlistat binds covalently to gastric and pancreatic lipases in the gut, preventing them from breaking down dietary triglycerides, so that a fraction of fat, described by Grokipedia as 25 to 30%, passes into stool [1][2]. Systemic absorption is minimal [1].

Roche developed orlistat from lipstatin, a compound produced by the bacterium Streptomyces toxytricini [1]. Xenical was approved in the US in April 1999 and the lower-dose Alli received OTC approval in 2007, according to Grokipedia [1]. A 2006 T Nation thread predicted OTC orlistat might be sold in mass market stores [9].

Forum discussions on T Nation from 2002 to 2017 include questions about combining orlistat with other drugs, its place in contest preparation stacks, and reports of diarrhea [20][14][21][10]. One poster argued bodybuilders already have strict diets and have less use for it [15].
